title: Reflection, refraction and lenses
examTip: Always measure angles of incidence and reflection from the normal, NOT from the surface itself. The normal is the dashed line at right angles to the surface. Measuring from the surface loses the most marks in ray diagram questions.
introTips: The normal is your reference line for all angle measurements. Draw it first, before adding any rays.
Refraction is about a change of speed at a boundary. If light slows down, it bends toward the normal.
Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser medium to a less dense one. It also needs a large angle.
A converging lens is thicker in the middle. It bends parallel rays inward to a focal point.
Real images can be projected onto a screen, but virtual images cannot. This difference comes up in exam questions.
intro: Glasses, contact lenses, cameras, telescopes, microscopes and endoscopes all use the same physics. So do the lenses in your own eyes. Light bends as it crosses the boundary between two materials. Reflection and refraction explain why you can see yourself in a mirror. They explain why a straw looks bent in a glass of water. They explain how optical fibres carry data around the world. Getting confident with ray diagrams and their rules gives you a solid base for optics questions. This topic shows up in more than one exam paper.

keyPoints.heading: Reflection and the law of reflection
keyPoints.content: Reflection happens when a wave, such as light, bounces off a surface. The key rule is the law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Both angles are always measured from the normal. This is an imaginary line at right angles to the surface. It is drawn where the light hits. On a ray diagram: - draw the normal first, as a dashed line - draw the incoming ray (incident ray) hitting the surface - draw the reflected ray leaving at the same angle, on the other side of the normal During reflection, the wave speed, frequency and wavelength do not change. Specular reflection: a smooth surface (a mirror) reflects rays in a single direction → a clear image. Diffuse reflection: a rough surface scatters reflected rays in many directions → no clear image (a matte finish).
writeBullets: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal)
Normal — a dashed line at right angles to the surface, where the light hits
Draw the normal first in any reflection or refraction diagram
Specular reflection — smooth surface → all rays reflect at the same angle → clear image (mirror)
Diffuse reflection — rough surface → rays scatter in all directions → no clear image

keyTerms.def: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection; both measured from the normal to the surface
An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface at the point of incidence; used as reference for angle measurements
Reflection from a smooth surface where all parallel rays reflect at the same angle, forming a clear image
Reflection from a rough surface where rays scatter in many directions, producing no clear image

keyPoints.memTip: In = Out. The angle IN (incidence) = the angle OUT (reflection).
keyPoints.tutor_note: The most common mistake in ray diagrams is measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal. Practise this again and again with worked examples.

keyPoints.heading: Refraction — light bending at a boundary
keyPoints.content: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary between two media. The media have different densities, and so different wave speeds. When light enters a denser medium (for example, glass or water), it slows down. It bends toward the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. When it enters a less dense medium (for example, from glass into air), it speeds up. It bends away from the normal. If light hits the boundary along the normal (0° incidence), it does not change direction. Only its speed changes. Frequency does not change during refraction, but wavelength does. This is because v = fλ, and the speed changes. This is Snell's law described in words. At GCSE you don't need to calculate the exact angle. But you need to draw and explain which way the light bends.
writeBullets: Refraction — a wave changes speed at a boundary. It changes direction too, unless it hits along the normal
Enters a denser medium (for example, air → glass) → slows down → bends toward the normal
Enters a less dense medium (for example, glass → air) → speeds up → bends away from the normal
Hits the boundary at 90° (along the normal) → no change in direction. Only the speed changes
Frequency unchanged; wavelength changes (v = fλ: speed changes, f stays the same)

keyTerms.def: The change in speed (and direction) of a wave as it crosses a boundary between two media; frequency unchanged
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal inside the new medium

keyPoints.memTip: Slower = toward the normal. Faster = away from the normal.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say the wave 'bends toward the surface' instead of 'toward the normal'. The normal is the reference line for both refraction and reflection.

keyPoints.heading: Total internal reflection
keyPoints.content: Total internal reflection (TIR) can happen when light in a denser medium meets a less dense medium. If the angle is greater than the critical angle, the light does not refract out. Instead, all of it reflects back inside the denser medium. At exactly the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary (90° from the normal). - Below the critical angle: most light refracts out, and some reflects. - Above the critical angle: all the light reflects inside. There is no refraction. TIR is the basis of optical fibres. Light pulses bounce along a glass fibre by TIR. This lets data travel long distances, losing very little energy. Optical fibres are used for broadband internet and medical endoscopes. TIR is also used in reflective road signs and bicycle reflectors.
writeBullets: Total internal reflection — all light reflects inside a denser medium when the angle > the critical angle
Critical angle — the angle at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary (90° to the normal)
Below the critical angle: refraction (mostly) happens. Above it: total internal reflection
TIR needs light to go from a denser to a less dense medium (for example, glass → air)
Optical fibre — uses TIR to carry light pulses along a glass or plastic fibre. Used in broadband and endoscopes

keyTerms.def: Complete reflection of light back into a denser medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
The angle of incidence at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary; above this, TIR occurs
A thin glass or plastic fibre that uses total internal reflection to transmit light signals along its length

keyPoints.memTip: TIR = Total Internal Reflection. It needs two things: a denser-to-less-dense boundary AND an angle > the critical angle.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up which way TIR can happen. It only happens going from denser to less dense, such as glass to air. It never happens the other way round.

keyPoints.heading: Lenses and ray diagrams
keyPoints.content: A converging (convex) lens is thicker in the middle. It refracts parallel rays so they meet at the focal point (F) on the other side. The distance from the lens to the focal point is the focal length. Ray diagrams for a converging lens use three standard rays: (1) a ray parallel to the principal axis → refracts through the focal point (2) a ray through the centre of the lens → passes straight through without bending (3) a ray through the focal point on the near side → refracts parallel to the axis Where these rays meet, an image forms. Real image: the rays really do converge. It can be projected onto a screen, and it is inverted (upside down). It forms when the object is beyond F. Virtual image: the rays only appear to spread out from a point. It cannot be projected, and it is upright. It forms when the object is between the lens and F, as in a magnifying glass. Uses: - magnifying glass: virtual, magnified - camera: real, diminished - projector: real, magnified - glasses for long-sight: a converging lens bends rays so they focus on the retina
writeBullets: Converging (convex) lens — thicker in the middle. Parallel rays refract through the focal point
Focal point (F) — where parallel rays meet after passing through a converging lens
Real image — rays really converge. Can be projected on a screen. Inverted. Object beyond F
Virtual image — rays only appear to diverge. Cannot be projected. Upright. Object between lens and F
Three standard rays: parallel→through F; through the centre→straight on; through the near F→parallel

keyTerms.def: A convex lens, thicker in the middle, that refracts parallel rays to meet at the focal point
The point where parallel rays converge after passing through a converging lens
Distance from the lens centre to the focal point
An image formed where light rays actually cross; can be projected on a screen; always inverted
An image from which rays appear to diverge; cannot be projected; always upright

keyPoints.memTip: Real image = rays REALLY meet. It can be projected and is inverted. Virtual = rays only VIRTUALLY meet. It is upright and cannot be projected.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ray diagrams are often examined. Practise drawing all three standard rays for different object distances. Then predict the image: real or virtual, magnified or diminished, upright or inverted.

0.question: A ray of light hits a mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! By the law of reflection, angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Both are 35°, measured from the normal.
0.wrongFeedback: The law of reflection says angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 35°. Remember, both angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface.

1.question: Light in glass hits the glass-air boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. What happens?
options: Total internal reflection. All the light reflects back into the glass
All the light refracts out into the air
The light speeds up and continues straight
The light is absorbed by the glass
1.correctFeedback: Correct! The light is going from a denser to a less dense medium. When the angle of incidence is more than the critical angle, total internal reflection happens. All the light bounces back inside the glass.
1.wrongFeedback: Beyond the critical angle, total internal reflection happens. No light refracts out. It all reflects back inside the glass. This is the idea behind optical fibres.

3.question: A converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. The object is between the lens and the focal point. What kind of image does it make?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! With the object between the lens and F, a magnifying glass makes a virtual image. It cannot be projected, and it is upright and magnified.
3.wrongFeedback: A magnifying glass (object between the lens and F) makes a virtual image. The rays don't really cross; they only appear to. The image is upright and magnified.

commonMistakes: Measuring angles of incidence and reflection from the surface instead of the normal. Always use the normal (the dashed line at right angles) as your reference.
Saying light bends away from the normal when it slows down. It bends toward the normal when it slows (entering a denser medium). It bends away when it speeds up.
Thinking total internal reflection can happen going from a less dense to a denser medium. It only happens going from denser to less dense (for example, glass to air).
Mixing up real and virtual images. Real images can be projected onto a screen, because the rays really converge. Virtual images cannot. Their rays only appear to converge when traced backwards.
Forgetting that frequency stays the same during refraction. The wavelength changes because the speed changes, but the frequency stays constant.
examTips: On ray diagrams, always draw the normal first as a dashed line, before adding rays. Without it, it is easy to mark angles wrongly.
For refraction questions, say whether the medium is denser or less dense. Say whether the speed goes up or down. Then say which way it bends: toward or away from the normal.
For TIR questions, always give two conditions. The boundary must go from denser to less dense, AND the angle must be more than the critical angle.
When asked to describe an image in a lens question, give all three properties. Real or virtual? Magnified or diminished? Upright or inverted?
Optical fibre questions often ask why TIR is useful. Say that light stays inside the fibre, with no energy lost through the sides. So data travels long distances efficiently.
revisionCardBullets: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal)
Normal — a line at right angles to the surface where the light hits. Drawn as a dashed line
Refraction — a wave changes speed at a boundary. Its direction changes unless it hits along the normal
Denser medium → slower → bends toward the normal
Less dense medium → faster → bends away from the normal
Frequency is unchanged in refraction. Wavelength changes
Total internal reflection — angle > critical angle, at a denser-to-less-dense boundary
Critical angle — at exactly this angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary
Optical fibre — uses TIR to carry light data. Used in broadband and endoscopes
Converging (convex) lens — parallel rays refract through the focal point
Real image — rays really converge. Can be projected. Inverted (object beyond F)
Virtual image — rays only appear to diverge. Cannot be projected. Upright (object between lens and F)
